claims.text: In situ high-resolution TEM/EDS combined with correlative atom probe tomography can reveal oxidation-induced elemental redistribution in the selected alloy's nanoprecipitates.
High-temperature oxidation induces significant elemental redistribution within the nanoprecipitates.
Oxidation enriches Al and Ti at the oxide-scale interface.
Al and Ti redistribution within the nanoprecipitates mediates improved oxidation resistance.
The Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy is produced by additive manufacturing and contains dual nanoprecipitation.
The additively manufactured alloy has a nanoscale distribution of precipitates.
Oxidation at approximately 900–1000 °C represents industrial high-temperature service conditions such as those in gas turbines and power plants.
Controlled atmospheres can isolate oxidation effects during the proposed high-temperature exposure.
Nanoprecipitates in the HEA matrix can undergo elemental partitioning during oxidation.
Al and Ti are oxidation-active elements in the proposed mechanism.
Al and Ti migrate to precipitate–matrix interfaces during high-temperature exposure.
Migration and interfacial enrichment of Al and Ti promote formation of protective oxide scales.
Formation of stable oxide layers such as Al2O3 can provide oxidation resistance at high temperature.
Oxidized regions will exhibit Al and Ti depletion in precipitate cores corresponding to enrichment at oxide scales.
Elemental segregation in the additively manufactured alloy will correlate with greater oxidation resistance than in cast or wrought material.
Cast and wrought versions of similar alloys do not exhibit the same extent of nanoprecipitate-induced elemental redistribution.
Cast and wrought versions of similar alloys have lower oxidation resistance than the additively manufactured alloy.
Temperature and atmosphere outside the proposed regime may produce different redistribution behavior.
Oxidation resistance is crucial for high-temperature alloys because oxidation can severely degrade mechanical properties.
Atom probe tomography can quantify atomic-scale composition while TEM/EDS can map nanoscale structural and elemental changes in the oxidized alloy.
